title: Trump vs. Cotton Clash Over Daylight Savings After Cell Phone Number Leak
body:
President Donald Trump ignited a fresh political spat on Saturday by publicly posting Senator Tom Cotton’s personal cell‑phone number and then launching a tirade against the Arkansas Republican’s opposition to a proposed daylight‑saving‑time reform. The exchange, which unfolded on Trump’s Truth Social platform, has drawn criticism from both parties for the former president’s use of personal data as a weapon and has revived a long‑standing debate over whether the United States should abandon the biannual clock change.

In a morning post that quickly went viral, Trump shared the nine‑digit number, accompanied by a caption that urged “the great American people” to call Cotton and demand he “stop blocking common‑sense legislation.” The president then proceeded to lambaste the senator, accusing him of “playing politics with the American worker” and “standing in the way of a simple fix that would give families an extra hour of daylight in the winter.” Cotton, a staunch ally of former President Trump on many issues, has nonetheless voted against the bipartisan “Sunshine Bill,” which would make daylight‑saving time permanent across the nation.

Cotton’s office responded within hours, confirming that the number posted was indeed his personal cell line and that the senator was “deeply concerned” about the breach of privacy. The senator’s communications director warned that the exposure could lead to “harassment and safety risks” for both Cotton and his family, and urged Trump’s team to remove the information immediately. The incident has prompted a flurry of legal commentary, with experts noting that while public officials’ contact information is often publicly listed, the deliberate dissemination of a private number for political pressure may contravene state harassment statutes and could expose the former president to civil liability.

The daylight‑saving controversy itself is not new. Since the Energy Policy Act of 2005 extended daylight‑saving time by four weeks, lawmakers have periodically introduced bills to make the schedule permanent, arguing that the shift disrupts sleep patterns, increases traffic accidents, and imposes economic costs. Supporters claim a year‑round schedule would boost retail sales, improve public safety and align the United States with most of Europe’s time‑keeping practices. Opponents, including Cotton, raise concerns about darker mornings in the winter months, particularly for schoolchildren and agricultural workers, and warn that a permanent shift could have unintended health consequences.

Trump’s latest foray into the daylight‑saving debate reflects a broader pattern of leveraging social media to influence legislative outcomes, a tactic he popularized during his 2016 campaign and continued throughout his presidency. By weaponizing personal data, he has once again blurred the line between political advocacy and intimidation. Critics argue that such tactics erode civil discourse and set a dangerous precedent for future office‑holders, while supporters contend that the former president is merely using every tool at his disposal to champion “common‑sense” policies.

The fallout from the episode is already rippling through Capitol Hill. Several members of the House Energy and Commerce Committee have called for an internal review of the incident, and a bipartisan group of senators is drafting a resolution to protect elected officials’ private contact information from being weaponized online. Meanwhile, civil liberties organizations have announced plans to file a complaint with the Federal Communications Commission, alleging that the public posting of a private number constitutes an unlawful “do‑not‑call” violation.

As the debate over permanent daylight‑saving time advances toward the upcoming congressional session, the Trump‑Cotton clash may prove to be a footnote, but it underscores the increasingly personal nature of modern political battles. Whether the Senate will finally move the Sunshine Bill forward—or whether the controversy will stall amid concerns over privacy and protocol—remains to be seen. What is clear is that the intersection of social‑media power, legislative agendas, and personal security will continue to shape the contours of American politics in the months ahead.
